newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton, Yeltsin square up for hard summit on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Yeltsin square up for hard summit on NATO.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The United States and Russia squared up on Tuesday for their toughest summit since the end of the Cold War, with hopes fading that they could reach a deal soon on the bitterly divisive issue of NATO enlargement.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin will try to resolve growing tensions over European security when they meet in Helsinki on Thursday and Friday.

NATO is preparing to invite a handful of countries from the former Soviet bloc to join the alliance, a move that Russia regards as a threat. Both sides have turned up the heat ahead of the summit, the 11th time Yeltsin and Clinton will have met.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Tuesday that NATO wanted a real partnership with Russia but that the 16-nation alliance would not be deterred from its plans or renege on its promise to the new democracies of Eastern Europe.
"NATO enlargement will remain on track," she said.
Yeltsin, on fighting form after months of illness and last year's heart surgery, spent Tuesday planning for the summit with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
On Monday, Yeltsin attacked NATO's plans to take in new members as a "blockade" and demanded that Russia be treated as an equal if a return to Cold War tensions was to be avoided.
"There has not been such a difficult meeting as this between me and an American president," said the Kremlin chief.

Yeltsin must be careful not to appear weak in front of his communist and nationalist critics at home. But Clinton, too, has said he expects the summit to be tough and U.S. officials are playing down any expectation of a breakthrough on NATO.
Primakov met Clinton in Washington on Monday and said afterwards Moscow would not change its opposition to enlargement, although it wanted proper relations with NATO.

The summit was delayed by one day after Clinton had to undergo surgery following a knee injury last week. Yeltsin, for so long the focus of health concerns, has made fun of the fact that Clinton will be either in a wheelchair or on crutches.
Nevertheless, the two men have established a good working relationship at previous summits. Helsinki will be their first meeting since they both won re-election last year.

The United States is hoping it can persuade Russia to accept, however grudgingly, that NATO enlargement will not present a threat to its security and that it can work -- as a major, well-respected power -- with an expanded alliance.
Time is running out since NATO leaders will invite several countries to start membership talks at a July summit in Madrid. Those are expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Yeltsin wants legally binding commitments in the NATO relationship, including guarantees that allied troops and nuclear arms will not be deployed in new member states.
NATO is offering Russia a new relationship through a special charter, which would give Moscow the right to consultation on security issues but no power of veto over the alliance's plans.

But the United States and its allies reject the Russian push for more binding commitments and Yeltsin's other demand -- that former Soviet republics, particularly the Baltic states, should be barred forever from NATO membership.
"The first new members will not be the last and we will exclude no European democracy from future consideration," Albright told reporters in Washington on Tuesday.
There are also problems with arms control, which is intimately linked with the NATO issue and with Russia's perception that it is surrounded by potential enemies.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) has offered to make major changes to a 1990 treaty on conventional forces in Europe, to meet Russian concerns about a Western arms buildup close to its borders.

Clinton is expected to discuss this and the deadlock over nuclear arms. The 1993 START-2 strategic arms pact, which provides for big cuts in the U.S. and Russian arsenals, has not come into force because the Russian Duma (parliament) views it as damaging to the country's security and has not ratified it.
U.S. officials have spoken of preparing for a possible new agreement that would go for even deeper cuts, but insist that the Duma must ratify START-2 first.

On the economic front, Yeltsin has complained bitterly that Russia is left out of key international groupings. Having given reformers the lead in a cabinet reshuffle this week, the Kremlin chief is expected to press that view hard in Helsinki.

Washington supports an increased Russian role in the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialised nations and may back its efforts to join other groupings like the World Trade Organisation and the Paris Club, which deals with debt.
